title: Sacramentals (CCC 1667–1673)
hookLine: holy water, blessings, medals, ashes: signs that prepare us for grace

lines: A MEDAL IN THE GLOVE BOX.
WATER IN A BOTTLE ON THE SILL.
A GRAY SMUDGE ON A FOREHEAD.
cards: At the back of a glove box, behind the registration and a tire gauge, a small medal of Saint Christopher on a chain, gone dull. Nobody remembers who put it there.

On a windowsill at home, a plastic bottle shaped like the Virgin Mary, half full of water. A farmer asks a priest to bless his tractor. On Ash Wednesday, strangers on a subway car share the same gray smudge.
None of these is a sacrament. All of them are something, and the Catechism has a word for that something.

teach.b: Sacramentals, the Catechism says, are sacred signs that bear a likeness to the sacraments: holy water, blessings, medals, ashes, the sign of the cross, a blessed candle. The difference matters.
Catholic teaching holds that the sacraments were instituted by Christ and give grace through the action itself. Sacramentals were instituted by the Church.
They don't give grace the way a sacrament does; they prepare a person to receive grace and cooperate with it, working through the prayer of the Church. They clear the ground.
A sacramental takes an ordinary moment, walking into a building, starting a car, falling asleep, and opens it toward God.
For well-disposed believers, the Catechism says, almost every event of life can be made holy this way. Among sacramentals, blessings come first, and Scripture has them too.
In Numbers, God gives Aaron's family words to bless the people with.

teach.h: THE LORD BLESS THEE, AND KEEP THEE.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims they begin: "The Lord bless thee, and keep thee." Blessings of people, meals, objects, places.
And a detail worth keeping: every baptized person, the Catechism says, is called to be a blessing, and to bless.

Some blessings belong to bishops and priests, but parents can bless their children, and a family can bless its table. One more thing it keeps clear: the power isn't in the water or the metal by itself.
A medal isn't a charm. It works, Catholic teaching says, through the Church's prayer and the faith of the person who uses it.

how: Catholics bless themselves with holy water on entering a church, wear blessed medals or scapulars, receive ashes on Ash Wednesday, and ask priests to bless homes, objects and people.

practice: If you have holy water at home, or you're near a church, dip your fingers and make the sign of the cross slowly, forehead, chest, left shoulder, right; if not, the slow sign of the cross alone, or a hand resting on your heart, can mark the moment.
Then let one ordinary part of your day come to mind, the drive, the desk, the dishes, and picture it marked the same way.

wordCard.voice: Sacramental. A sacred sign instituted by the Church, like holy water, a blessing, a medal or ashes, that prepares a person to receive grace, working through the Church's prayer. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: small holy things. Each one points past itself, toward God. See you tomorrow.
